analysis.investment_thesis: Exim Routes is a hypergrowth paper-recycling intermediary (revenue 4→121 Cr in 4 years, 134% CAGR) with optically attractive PEG of ~0.4 using recent profit growth. However, net profit has never once converted to positive operating cash flow—a disqualifying flaw for a Lynch buy.
key_strengths: Explosive revenue growth: 4→121 Cr in 4 years with profit inflecting from zero to INR 8 Cr in FY25
Outstanding ROE/ROCE of 54%/55% on existing capital base — capital-light intermediary model at its best
Low D/E of ~0.36 (borrowings INR 9 Cr vs equity INR 25 Cr); FII entry at 7.55% signals institutional awareness
key_risks: OCF negative all 5 years (0/5 positive); FY25 shows INR 8 Cr profit yet OCF = -5 Cr — classic working capital trap for fast-growing traders, but 5 consecutive years is alarming
Zero moat: paper-recycling facilitation is a pure commodity intermediary — any competitor can undercut; pricing power is near-zero
ROE will compress sharply: equity surged 4→25 Cr in FY25 (likely IPO proceeds), meaning the 54% ROE is backward-looking and unsustainable at this capital base
red_flags: Profits never convert to cash: INR 8 Cr net profit vs. -5 Cr OCF in FY25 suggests receivables/working capital are absorbing all earnings — a serious quality-of-earnings concern
Market cap (INR 248 Cr) is 2x TTM revenue (INR 121 Cr) for a trading/intermediary business with 8.3% EBITDA margins — that's a rich premium for a business with no proprietary IP or lock-in
Incorporated only April 2019 with zero profit track record before FY24 — the company has exactly one year of meaningful earnings history
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The growth numbers here look like a ten-bagger in the making — revenue up 30x in four years, profits finally appearing, ROE above 50%. As a Lynch fast-grower classifier, I'm always excited when a small company in an unglamorous niche (recycled paper!) posts triple-digit CAGRs. The story is simple: India's paper mills need a reliable aggregator of recyclable feedstock, and Exim Routes is building that platform. PEG ratio using recent ~100% earnings growth clocks in at roughly 0.38 — on paper, extraordinarily cheap.

But here's what kills the story for me: in five consecutive years of operation, this company has never generated a single rupee of positive operating cash flow. FY25 net profit was INR 8 Cr; operating cash flow was -5 Cr. That's a INR 13 Cr gap explained almost entirely by working capital ballooning alongside revenue. For a trading intermediary, this isn't a growth-stage luxury — it means the business may never be self-funding. The equity base tripled to INR 25 Cr in FY25 (likely IPO proceeds), which funds operations for now, but the cash burn means the 54% ROE is a mirage on the new capital. Until OCF turns consistently positive, this is a speculative story, not a Lynch-grade compounder.
